category.title: Combinatorics & Discrete Mathematics
category.description: Permutations, Combinations, Factorials, Pascal's Triangle, Lucas' Theorem for nCr modulo prime, and Inclusion-Exclusion Principle.

algorithms.title: Factorials & Inverse Factorials Precomputation
algorithms.summary: Precomputes Factorials `fact[i] = i!` and Inverse Factorials `invFact[i] = (i!)^(-1) % MOD` for instant O(1) combinatorics evaluations.
explanation: 1. Factorial Array: `fact[0] = 1`, `fact[i] = (fact[i-1] * i) % MOD`.
2. Fermat's Inverse: `invFact[N] = pow(fact[N], MOD - 2, MOD)`.
3. Linear Suffix Precomputation: `invFact[i-1] = (invFact[i] * i) % MOD` for `i` from N down to 1.
4. Precomputes both arrays up to N=10^6 in O(N) linear time.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Factorials up to N=5 (MOD = 10^9+7)
traceSteps: Enables instant O(1) computation of any nPr or nCr modulo MOD.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Precomputes factorials and inverse factorials for O(1) combinatorics queries.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When answering multiple combinatorics queries under modulo 10^9+7 or 998244353.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Competitive programming combinatorics, probability, graph counting.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(N) precomputation turns factorial division into fast O(1) multiplications.

algorithms.title: Permutations (nPr - Ordered Arrangements)
algorithms.summary: Calculates number of ordered arrangements of picking R items from N distinct items using formula nPr = n! / (n-r)!.
explanation: 1. Definition: Order matters! Arranging R items from N items.
2. Formula: `nPr = n! / (n - r)!`.
3. Modulo Formula: `nPr % MOD = (fact[n] * invFact[n - r]) % MOD`.
4. Invalid Bounds: Returns 0 if `r < 0` or `r > n`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace 5P2 (Arranging 2 items out of 5)
traceSteps: Using modulo arrays: (fact[5] * invFact[3]) % MOD = (120 * inv(6)) % MOD = 20.

wAnswers.whenToUse: When sequence order of items matters (e.g. passwords, seating arrangements).
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(1) query time using precomputed factorial arrays.

algorithms.title: Combinations (nCr) & Binomial Coefficients
algorithms.summary: Calculates number of unordered selections of R items from N distinct items using binomial formula nCr = n! / (r! * (n-r)!).
explanation: 1. Definition: Order does NOT matter! Choosing R items out of N.
2. Binomial Theorem: Coefficient of `x^(n-r) * y^r` in expansion `(x + y)^n` is `nCr`.
3. Formula: `nCr = n! / (r! * (n - r)!)`.
4. Modulo Multiplication: `nCr % MOD = (fact[n] * invFact[r] % MOD * invFact[n - r]) % MOD`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace 5C2 (Choosing 2 items out of 5)
traceSteps: Using precomputed inverse factorials: 120 * inv(2) * inv(6) mod MOD = 10.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes selection combinations in O(1) time.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When choosing subsets, committee formation, or grid path counts.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Grid unique paths DP, lottery probability, poker hand counts.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(1) time replaces O(R) multiplicative loops.

algorithms.title: Pascal's Triangle (DP Combination Table)
algorithms.summary: Computes binomial coefficients nCr via Dynamic Programming Pascal Triangle recurrence C[n][r] = C[n-1][r] + C[n-1][r-1] without division.
explanation: 1. Pascal Recurrence: `C(n, r) = C(n-1, r) + C(n-1, r-1)`.
2. Base Cases: `C(n, 0) = C(n, n) = 1` for all `n`.
3. Division-Free Advantage: Works for ANY modulo M (even non-primes where modular inverse does not exist!).
4. Precomputes entire 2D table `C[0..N][0..N]` in O(N^2) time.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Pascal Triangle up to Row 4

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes nCr modulo ANY arbitrary non-prime integer M without modular division.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When modulo M is not prime or when generating full Pascal triangle rows.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Pascal triangle queries, non-prime modulo combinatorics.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Simple additions avoid modular inverse prerequisites.

algorithms.title: nCr Modulo Prime (Fermat's Inverse Formula)
algorithms.summary: Evaluates nCr modulo prime P using Fermat's Little Theorem for modular inverse denominator division.
explanation: 1. Modulo Prime P: Fermat's Little Theorem states `inv(r!) = (r!)^(P-2) % P`.
2. Direct Computation: `nCr % P = (n! * (r!)^(P-2) * ((n-r)!)^(P-2)) % P`.
3. Multiplicative Approach: `nCr % P = ((n * (n-1) * ... * (n-r+1)) / (1 * 2 * ... * r)) % P`.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes large combinations modulo prime P without allocating memory for full factorial arrays.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When computing single queries of nCr modulo prime P.
wAnswers.whereUsed: On-demand combinatorics queries, modular math problems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(R + log P) single query without global precomputations.

algorithms.title: Lucas' Theorem (nCr Modulo Small Prime P)
algorithms.summary: Evaluates nCr modulo small prime P for huge inputs N, R up to 10^18 by breaking N and R into base-P digits.
explanation: 1. Base P Digits: Express N and R in base P: `N = n_k * P^k + ... + n_0`, `R = r_k * P^k + ... + r_0`.
2. Lucas Theorem: `nCr % P = (prod_{i=0..k} (n_i C r_i)) % P`.
3. Base Combination: Since `n_i, r_i < P`, evaluate `n_i C r_i % P` using simple modular formula.
4. Base Case: Returns 0 if any `r_i > n_i`.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Calculates nCr % P when N and R are up to 10^18 and P <= 10^5 is a small prime.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When N, R exceed standard array sizing limits.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(log_P N) base P digit reduction reduces 10^18 operations.

codeTemplates.code:
def nCr_small(n: int, r: int, p: int) -> int:
    if r < 0 or r > n: return 0
    num = den = 1
    for i in range(r):
        num = (num * (n - i)) % p
        den = (den * (i + 1)) % p
    return (num * pow(den, p - 2, p)) % p

def lucas_nCr(n: int, r: int, p: int) -> int:
    if r == 0: return 1
    ni = n % p
    ri = r % p
    return (lucas_nCr(n // p, r // p, p) * nCr_small(ni, ri, p)) % p

algorithms.title: Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion (PIE)
algorithms.summary: Computes cardinality of set union by adding individual set sizes, subtracting pair intersections, adding triplet intersections, and continuing for all 2^K bitmask subsets.
explanation: 1. Union Formula: `|A1 U A2 U ... U Ak| = sum(|Ai|) - sum(|Ai ∩ Aj|) + sum(|Ai ∩ Aj ∩ Ak|) - ...`.
2. Bitmask Strategy: Iterate `mask` from 1 to `2^K - 1` representing all subsets.
3. Parity Rule: If `mask` has odd number of set bits, add subset intersection. If even, subtract subset intersection.

exampleTrace.title: Trace PIE to count numbers <= 30 divisible by 2, 3, or 5

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds union size of multiple overlapping condition sets in O(2^K) time.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When counting elements satisfying at least one of K conditions.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Derangements counting, co-prime counting, constrained grid paths.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Solves complex set union counting without iterating through all elements.
